title: CLI Tools
subtitle: Building command-line tools with process.argv, readline, and formatted output
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Developers spend a lot of time in the terminal. CLI tools automate repetitive tasks — code generation, data processing, deployments, file management — far faster than GUIs.
whyItExists.solution: Node.js is excellent for CLI tools: fast startup, built-in file system access, npm ecosystem. process.argv reads command-line arguments. readline handles interactive prompts. stdout/stderr control output. The bin field in package.json registers a global command.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Build scripts, code generators, data migration tools, project scaffolding, automation workflows, developer utilities.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For long-running daemons with network I/O, a server process is more appropriate. For GUI-heavy tools, consider Electron or a web UI.

explainModes.beginner: A CLI tool is a program you run from the terminal. process.argv is an array of the command and its arguments: node script.js hello → process.argv = ['node', 'script.js', 'hello']. You read process.argv[2] to get the first user argument. process.stdout.write prints without a newline. process.exit(0) ends the program.
explainModes.simple: process.argv: array ['node', 'scriptPath', ...userArgs]. User args start at index 2. Parse flags: const verbose = process.argv.includes('--verbose'). Parse values: const idx = process.argv.indexOf('--name'); const name = idx !== -1 ? process.argv[idx+1] : null. ANSI colors: '\x1b[32mgreen\x1b[0m'. readline: create interface with createInterface, call question() for prompts, close() when done. Exit codes: 0 = success, 1+ = error.
explainModes.standard: Arg parsing libraries: minimist (tiny, no-dep), yargs (full-featured: flags, commands, validation, help), commander (Express-style CLI). package.json bin field: '"bin": { "mytool": "./bin/cli.js" }' — npm install -g registers the command globally. Shebang: #!/usr/bin/env node at top of the file — tells the OS to run it with Node. chmod +x cli.js — make it executable. stdout vs stderr: use console.error() or process.stderr.write() for errors — this allows piping stdout while seeing errors.
explainModes.technical: Interactive prompts: readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout }). rl.question(prompt, callback) or rl.question(prompt) → Promise (Node 17+). rl.close() — close when done or stdin stays open. Detecting TTY: process.stdout.isTTY — true in terminal, false when piped. Use this to disable color output when output is redirected to a file. Signal handling: process.on('SIGINT', handler) for Ctrl+C cleanup. process.on('SIGTERM', handler) for kill signal (graceful shutdown).
explainModes.deepDive: Inquirer.js: advanced CLI prompts — checkbox, list, password, editor. Used by many scaffolding tools. chalk/kleur: ANSI color libraries with no-color detection. ora: spinner for async operations. boxen: boxes around terminal output. listr2: task list with progress. All these build on process.stdout/stderr and ANSI escape codes. ANSI codes: \x1b[32m = green, \x1b[31m = red, \x1b[0m = reset, \x1b[1m = bold, \x1b[2m = dim. NO_COLOR env var: de-facto standard to disable colors — check process.env.NO_COLOR.

questions.question: What does `process.argv.slice(2)` do and why?
options: It removes the first two items from process.argv in place
It returns a new array without the first two elements. process.argv[0] is always 'node' and process.argv[1] is the script path — the user's actual arguments start at index 2
It parses the first two arguments as flags
It limits argv to two arguments maximum
questions.explanation: process.argv always starts with ['node', '/path/to/script.js', ...userArgs]. The first two elements are the Node.js executable path and the script path — not user input. slice(2) creates a new array starting from index 2, which contains only what the user typed after the script name. This is the standard idiom for processing CLI arguments.

faq.q: How do I make my Node.js script run as a global command (e.g., `mytool` instead of `node tool.js`)?
faq.a: 1. Add a shebang line at the top: `#!/usr/bin/env node`. 2. Make it executable: `chmod +x cli.js` (on Mac/Linux). 3. Add to package.json: `"bin": { "mytool": "./cli.js" }`. 4. Run `npm install -g .` (installs globally from the current directory). Now `mytool` runs your script. For sharing, publish to npm — `npm install -g your-package` makes it available globally.
